query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-deformation induced lattice distortions facilitate shear transformation pathways that trigger secondary phase nucleation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in the as-cast, high-temperature BCC state with minimal pre-existing lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled cold rolling deformation (e.g., 20% thickness reduction) to introduce dislocations and lattice distortions before subjecting the material to annealing at 600–700°C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Cold rolling performed under controlled conditions followed by identical annealing in inert atmosphere; comparisons made between deformed and undeformed samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced dislocation density, grain boundary misorientations, and local lattice distortions as determined by EBSD and TEM.
generation.mechanism: Pre-deformation creates local shear and lattice distortions that lower the nucleation barrier for phase transformation via shear mechanisms (akin to the Pitsch mechanism observed in related HEAs), leading to preferential nucleation of secondary phases (such as FCC or σ-phase) along deformed regions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-deformed samples will display an earlier onset of secondary phase formation and a distinct crystallographic texture (e.g., orientation relationships deviating from the parent BCC), with an increase in phase fraction of secondary phases by roughly 10–20% compared to undeformed samples.
generation.baseline: As-cast, undeformed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples annealed under identical conditions, maintaining a more uniform BCC structure.
generation.boundary: The effect is contingent on an optimal level of deformation; too little deformation (<5%) may not produce measurable distortions, while excessive deformation may lead to amorphization, invalidating the shear transformation mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Determining the optimal deformation level and isolating shear transformation effects from general defect-enhanced diffusion remains challenging.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples—one pre-deformed by 20% cold rolling and one undeformed—and anneal both at 650°C for 1 hour. Use in situ diffraction (e.g., synchrotron XRD) and EBSD to compare phase transformation onset temperatures, orientation relationships, and phase fractions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-deformed samples do not show a statistically significant difference in phase transformation kinetics or orientation relationships compared to undeformed samples, or if the transformation pathway is identical, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

AbstractThe solid state phase transformation kinetics of as-cast and cold rolling deformed Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys have been investigated by the thermal expansion method. The phase transformed volume fractions are determined from the thermal expansion curve using the lever rule method, and the deformed sample exhibits a much higher transformation rate. Two kinetic parameters, activation energy (E) and kinetic exponent (n) are determined using Kissinger– Akahira–Sunose (KAS) and Johnson–Mehl–Avrami (JMA) method, respectively. Results show that a pre-deformed sample shows a much lower activation energy and higher kinetic exponent compared with the as-cast sample, which are interpreted based on the deformation induced defects that can promote the nucleation and growth process during phase transformation.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, phase transformation, kinetics, deformation, thermal expansion

papers.title: Microstructure Evolution of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 High Entropy Alloy during Powder Preparation, Laser Powder Bed Fusion, and Microp
papers.approach: Powder production via gas atomization, subsequent L-PBF and microplasma spraying processing, followed by systematic annealing with characterization by XRD, SEM, EDS, and DTA.
papers.findings: The as-atomized material forms a supersaturated BCC (with partial B2 ordering) that shows minor Mo- and Al-rich segregations. Annealing induces increased elemental segregation accompanied by elastic stress buildup, eventually leading to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution and the formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. A maximum in microhardness is observed at intermediate annealing (around 600 °C), likely due to elastic stress from segregation.
papers.mechanism: Elemental segregation creates lattice distortions and elastic stresses between regions of varying chemistry; once a critical stress or misfit threshold is reached, nucleation of intermetallic phases (e.g., σ-phase) is triggered via diffusion-controlled processes.

papers.title: Orientation Relationships in Al0.7CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Detailed microstructural and crystallographic analysis using EBSD and SEM to study phase transformation from an initial BCC state to partially transformed FCC microstructures.
papers.findings: The initial cast alloy in the BCC state partially transforms into FCC with a predominance of the Pitsch orientation relationship during nucleation. Deviations from the ideal Pitsch OR are linked to lattice distortions caused by chemical inhomogeneity and the formation of ordered B2 regions.
papers.mechanism: Shear-driven transformation that is sensitive to lattice distortions produced by atomic size differences and segregation, contributing to the heterogeneous nucleation of new phases.

papers.title: Phase transformation and strengthening of the gas-atomized FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder during annealing.
papers.approach: Annealing experiments combined with microhardness testing and activation energy estimation, supported by XRD and SEM/EDS analyses.
papers.findings: An initial low activation energy (0.65 eV) for the onset of decomposition shifts to a higher value (≈2.6 eV) upon sigma-phase formation. The alloy exhibits increased hardness when annealing induces sufficient segregation and elastic stress, with sigma-phase nucleation correlated with semi-coherent boundary formation.
papers.mechanism: A diffusion-controlled process in which initial quenched vacancies and elemental segregation lower the energy barrier for decomposition; as elastic stresses build up from segregation-induced lattice misfit, nucleation of the sigma phase is triggered.

papers.title: Influence of Cold Rolling on the Phase Transformation Kinetics of an Al0.5CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Cold rolling to introduce defects followed by thermal expansion measurements; kinetic parameters were extracted using the Kissinger–Akahira–Sunose (KAS) and Johnson–Mehl–Avrami (JMA) methods.
papers.findings: Pre-deformed (cold-rolled) samples exhibit a lower activation energy and higher kinetic exponent compared with as-cast samples, indicating enhanced nucleation and growth rates during phase transformation.
papers.mechanism: Deformation-induced defects and strain increase atomic mobility and act as preferential nucleation sites, thereby accelerating phase evolution from the supersaturated state.

papers.title: Microstructure and Thermal Analysis of Metastable Intermetallic Phases in High-Entropy Alloy CoCrFeMo0.85Ni.
papers.approach: Combination of differential thermal analysis (DTA) and microstructural characterization to track the emergence and evolution of metastable intermetallic phases during thermal cycling.
papers.findings: A mixture of metastable phases (μ and σ) emerges around 800 °C; these phases are associated with elemental partitioning (especially Mo and Cr) and grow via segregation-controlled spinodal decomposition, with subsequent coarsening under further thermal exposure.
papers.mechanism: Segregative spinodal decomposition driven by differential element diffusion leads to localized chemical enrichment and intermetallic formation, with the process being highly sensitive to thermal history and diffusion kinetics.

established: High-entropy alloys often solidify in a supersaturated, high-temperature BCC (or BCC/B2) state that decomposes upon cooling or annealing into a mixture of phases such as σ, B2, and FCC.
Elemental segregation and the concomitant lattice distortion produce elastic stresses that can drive phase transformation when a critical threshold is reached.
Kinetic factors (e.g., diffusion rates, defect densities) significantly influence the activation energies and pathways of phase transformations in these alloys.

approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of a supersaturated BCC state that later decomposes into secondary phases (σ and B2) as segregation and elastic stresses build, with corresponding changes in hardness.

approaches_tried.approach: Cold deformation (cold rolling) to modify the microstructure
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced nucleation kinetics and lower activation energy for phase transformation due to increased defect density, leading to accelerated phase evolution.

approaches_tried.outcome: Identification of transformation temperatures and the role of diffusion-limited segregation in phase decomposition, particularly in metastable systems.

mechanisms: Elastic stress buildup from segregation-induced lattice misfit, which once exceeding a critical threshold, triggers the nucleation of secondary phases.
Shear transformation mechanisms governed by orientation relationships (e.g., Pitsch OR) that are sensitive to local lattice distortions and chemical inhomogeneities.
Defect-enhanced diffusion and segregation kinetics that control the transition from a supersaturated solid solution to equilibrium or metastable intermetallic phases.
disagreements: There is debate regarding whether the dominant nucleation mechanism is primarily driven by elastic stress from segregation versus shear-transformation dynamics influenced by atomic size mismatches.

Some studies emphasize kinetic barriers and diffusion controls (with distinct activation energies), while others highlight thermodynamic predictions (e.g., CALPHAD-based phase boundaries) that sometimes do not align perfectly with experimental observations.
open_questions: What are the precise factors (e.g., magnitude of elastic stress, degree of segregation) that set the onset of phase decomposition in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7?
How do subtle compositional differences and processing histories (e.g., cooling rate, pre-deformation) affect the balance between competing phase formation pathways (σ, B2, FCC)?
What is the quantitative relationship between lattice misfit, internal elastic stress, and the activation barrier for nucleation of secondary phases in these alloys?
opportunities: Perform controlled annealing experiments on Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 comparing a baseline rapidly cooled, undeformed BCC microstructure to samples intentionally pre-deformed to introduce defects. This would allow isolation of the effect of elastic stresses and segregation on phase stability.

Implement in situ diffraction or microscopy (e.g., high-energy synchrotron XRD, in situ TEM) during cooling and annealing to monitor real-time evolution of segregation, elastic strain, and phase nucleation.

Combine CALPHAD predictions with systematic thermal treatments to map out the precise temperature and time regimes where the transition from a high-temperature BCC phase to secondary phases occurs, providing a rigorous test of the segregation–stress hypothesis.

directions.direction: Elastic stress buildup from elemental segregation triggers phase nucleation.
directions.type: Mechanism study via heat treatment and in‐situ diffraction.
directions.assessment: This direction directly probes how lattice misfit from segregated elements (e.g., Al, Cr) induces elastic stresses that, when exceeding a critical threshold, trigger the nucleation of secondary phases. It is supported by microhardness and XRD evidence and is experimentally feasible by comparing annealing regimes.

directions.direction: Diffusion‐controlled elemental segregation leading to secondary phase formation.
directions.assessment: This approach tests whether different diffusion kinetics among the alloy’s constituents cause local compositional fluctuations which in turn nucleate secondary phases. Prior studies using EDS mapping and thermal analysis support this, and controlled annealing experiments can isolate segregation effects.

directions.direction: The role of quenched vacancy concentration and deformation‐induced defects in lowering activation barriers for phase transformation.
directions.type: Processing (cooling rate and mechanical pre-treatment) and kinetic studies.
directions.assessment: This strategy examines how rapid quenching and/or pre-deformation can create high vacancy concentrations, reducing activation energies for diffusion‐driven phase change. The evidence on low activation energies and defect‐enhanced kinetics makes this an attractive and testable hypothesis.

directions.direction: Shear transformation mediated by lattice distortions from atomic size mismatches.
directions.assessment: This avenue investigates whether pre-imposed or intrinsic lattice distortions (e.g., due to atomic size differences) promote shear transformation pathways (e.g., via Pitsch orientation relationships) that enable the nucleation of FCC or intermetallic phases. It is supported by crystallographic studies and is testable by comparing deformed and undeformed samples.

directions.direction: Thermodynamic‐kinetic mapping using in situ diffraction during controlled cooling.
directions.assessment: By merging CALPHAD predictions with real-time diffraction studies during cooling, one can assess whether the observed range of phases corresponds to expected thermodynamic boundaries modified by kinetic effects. Although promising, this approach is more complex in isolating a single mechanistic cause.
